title: Hyper-V Host Sustained Physical CPU Overload
exclusions: Measures only the `_Total` instance of `Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor\% Total Run Time`, the Microsoft-recommended counter for total non-idle time across physical logical processors. A row means at least four valid 60-second samples in one closed five-minute bucket and every sample exceeded 90 percent. It does not measure standard `Processor\% Processor Time`, per-VM or per-vCPU demand, root-partition CPU, interrupt/DPC contribution, CPU ready/wait, NUMA placement, memory, disk, network, thermal throttling, guest application latency, or future capacity. `_Total` is an aggregate and can hide one hot logical processor. The over-90 threshold comes from Microsoft bottleneck guidance; five-minute persistence, sample completeness, local index/source type, inventory, and exceptions are deployment policy. Missing, malformed, duplicate, delayed, or stale samples are data-quality findings, not low CPU. This UC does not migrate VMs, change vCPU allocation, or modify power/firmware settings.
evidence: After deployment, retain the `hyperv_host_sustained_physical_cpu_overload` saved search, ACL, five-minute schedule, dispatch rows, alerts, and throttle state; effective `[perfmon://HyperVLogicalProcessor]` input and deployment assignment; raw 60-second events with object, counter, `_Total` instance, percent Value, host, event/index time, and source type; expected-host inventory and exception lookup revisions; sample-coverage and duplicate/invalid-value reports; positive, negative, and 90-percent boundary tests; correlated per-logical-processor, root/guest virtual-processor, interrupt/DPC, VM workload, power/thermal, memory, storage, and network evidence; change/incident disposition; and post-action recovery buckets. These artifacts show sustained aggregate physical CPU busy time, not root cause or application impact. This documentation-only review collected no counter, ran no search, caused no load, and produced no alert or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Fix dispatch at 2026-07-29T03:10:00Z. In an isolated index, ingest five one-minute `_Total` samples for `hv-lab-01` in the closed 03:00–03:05 bucket with exact object/counter/source type and Values 91, 94, 96, 93, and 92. Add an active inventory row and no exception. Expect exactly one row for bucket 03:00 with `sample_count=5`, `min_cpu_pct=91`, `avg_cpu_pct=93.2`, `max_cpu_pct=96`, `threshold_pct=90`, and persistence `all_collected_samples_over_threshold`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and require zero rows when Values are 90,91,92,93,94 (minimum equals 90); 89,91,92,93,94; only three over-90 samples; wrong object, counter, instance, source type, or inactive inventory; any nonnumeric, negative, or over-100 sample after validation; and a valid sustained bucket with an exact active host exception. An exception expiring exactly at dispatch or lacking reason/ticket/owner must not suppress. Duplicate timestamps and gaps must surface in companion sample-health checks; a missing sample must never be replaced by zero.

dataSources: Native Windows Performance Monitor input on each in-scope Hyper-V host, sampled every 60 seconds with object `Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor`, counter `% Total Run Time`, and instance `_Total`. Splunk's perfmon input emits searchable `object`, `counter`, `instance`, and numeric `Value` fields. Local `index=perfmon` and `sourcetype=perfmon:HyperV_Logical_Processor` are deployment conventions; the source-type spelling is also documented by the archived Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Hyper-V, but no current archived add-on dependency is implied. Required fields are `_time, _indextime, host, sourcetype, object, counter, instance, Value`. Expected-host and exception CSVs are deployment-owned.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) for supported Windows collection context plus a deployment-owned native perfmon input/search app. The Windows add-on does not automatically guarantee this exact Hyper-V stanza. The archived Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Hyper-V documents the legacy source type and counter-set input but is reference-only; validate exact counter availability and fields on supported current hosts and forwarders.
spl:
index=perfmon sourcetype="perfmon:HyperV_Logical_Processor" object="Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor" counter="% Total Run Time" instance="_Total" earliest=-10m@m latest=@m
| eval cpu_pct=tonumber(Value)
| where cpu_pct>=0 AND cpu_pct<=100
| lookup hyperv_host_cpu_inventory.csv host OUTPUT monitor_enabled owner cluster_name service_name runbook monitor_from_epoch monitor_until_epoch
| eval monitor_from_epoch=tonumber(monitor_from_epoch), monitor_until_epoch=tonumber(monitor_until_epoch), inventory_active=if(lower(trim(monitor_enabled))="true" AND monitor_from_epoch<=now() AND monitor_until_epoch>now(),1,0)
| where inventory_active=1
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS sample_count dc(_time) AS distinct_sample_times min(cpu_pct) AS min_cpu_pct avg(cpu_pct) AS avg_cpu_pct max(cpu_pct) AS max_cpu_pct max(_indextime) AS last_indexed by _time host owner cluster_name service_name runbook
| where sample_count>=4 AND distinct_sample_times>=4 AND min_cpu_pct>90
| lookup hyperv_host_cpu_exceptions.csv host OUTPUT exception_until_epoch reason AS exception_reason ticket exception_owner
| eval exception_until_epoch=tonumber(exception_until_epoch), exception_active=if(exception_until_epoch>now() AND len(exception_reason)>0 AND len(ticket)>0 AND len(exception_owner)>0,1,0)
| where exception_active=0
| eval min_cpu_pct=round(min_cpu_pct,2), avg_cpu_pct=round(avg_cpu_pct,2), max_cpu_pct=round(max_cpu_pct,2), threshold_pct=90, window_seconds=300, persistence="all_collected_samples_over_threshold", observation_semantics="aggregate_physical_logical_processor_busy_percent_not_guest_or_root_cause", use_case_id="UC-2.2.6"
| table _time host cluster_name min_cpu_pct avg_cpu_pct max_cpu_pct sample_count distinct_sample_times threshold_pct window_seconds persistence owner service_name runbook last_indexed observation_semantics use_case_id
| sort 0 -avg_cpu_pct host
description: Runs every five minutes over closed five-minute buckets of 60-second host samples. It emits one row per inventoried Hyper-V host only when at least four distinct `_Total` physical logical-processor samples exist and the minimum `% Total Run Time` is greater than 90 percent, preserving minimum, average, maximum, and sample count.
value: Sustained aggregate physical CPU saturation can delay every VM on a host and undermine maintenance, failover, and service objectives. A conservative persistence rule gives virtualization and capacity teams an actionable host signal while retaining enough sample and ownership context to distinguish guest demand, root-partition overhead, interrupt load, power constraints, and telemetry defects.
implementation: On each supported Hyper-V host, deploy a native Splunk perfmon stanza for exact English object `Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor`, exact counter `% Total Run Time`, `_Total`, `useEnglishOnly=1`, and 60-second interval. Prove object/counter/value/units against Windows Performance Monitor and validate source type, host, event time, index time, duplicate rate, and expected sample cadence. Save the SPL every five minutes; require at least four distinct samples and every valid sample over Microsoft's 90-percent overload boundary. Alert per host/bucket, keep sample-health separate, and diagnose with per-LP, root/guest VP, interrupt/DPC, workload, power, memory, disk, and network evidence before any capacity action.
visualization: Place collection trust first: expected-host coverage, last sample age, samples per five-minute bucket, duplicate timestamps, invalid/out-of-range values, object/counter/source-type drift, and indexing delay. Then show current sustained hosts, minimum/average/maximum percent, cluster and owner; a 24-hour 60-second line chart with the 90-percent boundary; a heatmap by host and bucket; and recurrence by cluster/change window. Drill down to per-logical-processor `% Total Run Time`, `% Guest Run Time`, `% Hypervisor Run Time`, root/guest virtual processors, interrupt/DPC, VM inventory/load, thermal/power, and service latency. Never chart missing samples as zero or call `_Total` a per-VM metric.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. No accelerated CIM dataset is asserted to preserve the exact Hyper-V physical logical-processor object/counter/instance, native 60-second sample values, sample completeness, and all-samples-over-90 persistence semantics. Raw perfmon events remain primary.

knownFalsePositives:
A row means the collected `_Total` physical logical-processor busy percentage stayed above 90 for every valid sample in the bucket. The condition can be intentional, but it is not fabricated by an expected workload.

1. **Approved load, failover, or capacity test** — A performance engineer may intentionally saturate a lab or production test host. Verify exact host/cluster, tool/workload, operator, change/test ID, expected CPU profile, service safeguards, start/end, and rollback. Use the exact-host exception lookup only for the bounded approved interval.

2. **Planned host drain or VM evacuation wave** — Migration coordination and concentrated workloads can temporarily load source or destination hosts. Correlate cluster drain state, VM moves, source/destination ownership, concurrency, change window, and service probes. Keep capacity impact visible; do not suppress the entire cluster.

3. **Known batch, backup, antivirus, patch, or inventory workload** — Host or guest activity can legitimately drive aggregate CPU. Identify the exact process/VM/job, schedule, owner, completion objective, per-VM/root CPU split, and business impact. Recurrence above 90 percent is still capacity evidence and should be tuned through workload policy, not denied.

4. **Root-partition driver, interrupt, or DPC load** — Network/storage drivers, VMQ/RSS configuration, or device activity can consume CPU outside a single guest. Compare root virtual-processor, `Processor\% Interrupt Time`, `% DPC Time`, adapters, drivers, and hardware events. Route to host/network/storage engineering rather than adding VM capacity blindly.

5. **Power, firmware, thermal, or processor-capacity change** — Firmware policy, power plan, throttling, disabled cores, or hardware maintenance can reduce available compute and make normal demand exceed 90 percent. Correlate effective logical-processor inventory, clock/thermal/power telemetry, firmware/change, and hardware health.

6. **Duplicate or delayed performance samples** — Duplicate input assignments, clock problems, or backfill can inflate sample count or place values in the wrong bucket. Compare distinct `_time`, `_indextime`, source, forwarder, effective stanza, and known canary. The primary requires four distinct times, while source-health must expose duplicates and delay.

**Suppression mechanism:** the `hyperv_host_cpu_exceptions.csv` lookup matches exact `host` and requires future numeric `exception_until_epoch`, nonempty reason, ticket, and exception owner. It suppresses notification only after a complete sustained bucket. Expired/malformed exceptions, missing/late/duplicate samples, individual hot logical processors, invalid values, and unreviewed production saturation remain visible in companion panels.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact physical-CPU claim

Assign Hyper-V, Failover Clustering, Windows/hardware, capacity, network, storage, workload, Splunk data/content, and incident/change owners. Inventory every expected host by canonical Splunk `host`, cluster, processor/socket/core/logical-processor topology, Windows build, firmware, power policy, critical workloads, owner, and maintenance state. Use supported hosts and forwarders qualified in the deployment; this review ran no version combination, so it makes no `splunkVersions` assertion. The collection identity needs local performance-counter access only. Restrict input and exception changes; grant the search role perfmon-index, lookup, scheduling, and approved notification access.

Microsoft states that root/child Task Manager or standard Processor CPU counters do not represent actual physical CPU usage on Hyper-V. It directs operators to `Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor(*)\% Total Run Time`, the total non-idle time of logical processors. Microsoft's bottleneck guidance says `_Total` over 90 percent means the host is overloaded and recommends more processing power or moving VMs. This UC therefore replaces the former 85-percent threshold and does not use the generic `Processor\% Processor Time` counter.

The native counter is percent, nominally 0–100 for `_Total`. `_Total` is the aggregate/average instance; it can hide a single hot LP. The five-minute rule is local persistence: with a 60-second input, at least four distinct valid samples must exist and the minimum must be strictly greater than 90. Exactly 90 does not fire. A complete expected bucket is five samples, so four is a tolerance, not permission to ignore chronic collection gaps.

## Step 1 — Configure the exact native perfmon input

Deploy a version-controlled local app to each Hyper-V host with an input equivalent to:

```ini
[perfmon://HyperVLogicalProcessor]
object = Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor
counters = % Total Run Time;% Guest Run Time;% Hypervisor Run Time
instances = *
interval = 60
useEnglishOnly = 1
mode = single
index = perfmon
sourcetype = perfmon:HyperV_Logical_Processor
disabled = 0
```

Splunk requires exact existing object/counter names and supports one perfmon stanza per object, semicolon-separated counters, selected instances, interval, and `useEnglishOnly`. The index and source type above are local; the source-type spelling follows the archived Hyper-V add-on for migration convenience. Splunkbase 742 is optional collection context, not the source of this custom stanza. Collecting `*` enables diagnostic per-LP and guest/hypervisor splits, but the primary search uses only `_Total` `% Total Run Time`. If ingest cost requires narrower collection, include `_Total` explicitly and retain a documented on-demand per-LP path.

On every Windows language/build cohort, compare `typeperf -qx` and Performance Monitor > Add Counters with raw Splunk events. Prove exact object, counter, `_Total`, `Value`, percent units, 60-second cadence, host identity, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Confirm `useEnglishOnly=1` behavior. Record any localized or renamed counter behavior before rollout; do not silently change the search to a partial cohort.

Create `hyperv_host_cpu_inventory.csv` with unique `host,monitor_enabled,owner,cluster_name,service_name,runbook,monitor_from_epoch,monitor_until_epoch`. Reconcile with cluster/host inventory daily. Create `hyperv_host_cpu_exceptions.csv` with `host,exception_until_epoch,reason,ticket,exception_owner`. Reject wildcards, duplicates, invalid times, and indefinite expiry.

## Step 2 — Establish sample-health controls

Build an inventory-first search that counts distinct `_time` values per expected host and five-minute bucket. Report zero through three samples, more than expected, duplicate timestamps, values outside 0–100, nonnumeric/null Value, source-type/object/counter/instance drift, future event time, excessive `_indextime-_time`, hosts not in inventory, and inventory hosts never observed. Show coverage above the CPU panel.

A Splunk event can be duplicated by overlapping deployment apps, Windows forwarding architecture, or reindexing. `dc(_time)` reduces false completeness but cannot prove one source. Track `_cd`, source, forwarder, stanza, and index path in source health. Do not fill missing minutes with zero, carry values forward, or average across hosts.

Measure event volume and search runtime for all LPs/counters. If scale is material, route a separately governed metric-index copy and use `mstats`, but do not claim equivalence until metric name, percent unit, dimensions, cadence, and boundary fixtures produce identical findings. No CIM/tstats substitute is asserted here.

## Step 3 — Save and understand the sustained search

Save the supplied SPL as `hyperv_host_sustained_physical_cpu_overload` and schedule every five minutes after the closed bucket is expected to index, using `earliest=-10m@m latest=@m`. It selects the exact source type/object/counter/instance, converts `Value`, rejects invalid range, requires active expected inventory, and bins into five minutes.

`stats` preserves sample count, distinct times, minimum, average, maximum, and latest index time per host/bucket. Requiring `sample_count>=4`, `distinct_sample_times>=4`, and `min_cpu_pct>90` means every accepted collected minute was over the Microsoft boundary. It is intentionally stricter than average above 90. The exception applies afterward. Trigger one alert per host/bucket and throttle/update the same host incident while consecutive buckets continue; retain each bucket as evidence.

Route by cluster, service, and owner. Include all summary values, source-health link, change window, top per-VM/root CPU drilldowns, and runbook. Use high urgency for critical clusters only after validating service policy; `criticality=high` reflects host-wide blast radius, not an automatic incident severity for every lab.

## Step 4 — Validate percent, persistence, and edge cases

Run the fixed positive fixture and assert exact minimum/average/maximum, counts, and bucket time. Run every negative independently. Add sample sequences for all 90, 90.000/90.001, four valid over-90 samples, three samples, duplicate same-time events, six samples, values 0/100, negative/101/null/text, event at bucket edges, late indexing, host case policy, inventory start/end equality, exception expiry equality, and clock skew.

On a nonproduction host, compare five consecutive Performance Monitor readings with raw Splunk and the bucket result. Use an already approved load test if available; do not run an uncontrolled CPU burner on production merely to create evidence. Independently calculate min/average/max. Verify alert trigger, throttle, dashboard, lookup replication, scheduler skips, peer failure, and recovery after values return at or below 90.

Test host reboot, forwarder restart, deployment change, counter unavailable, Hyper-V role removal, maintenance inventory expiry, cluster rename, and duplicate stanza. Every case must either preserve correct primary behavior or create sample-health status. Keep `status=draft` until virtualization, hardware/capacity, workload, and Splunk owners accept versions, units, cadence, persistence, fixtures, source health, alerting, and response.

## Step 5 — Diagnose before changing capacity

Responder sequence: (1) verify inventory, source health, distinct samples, raw percent, event/index time, and current Performance Monitor; (2) inspect individual logical processors for imbalance hidden by `_Total`; (3) split `% Guest Run Time` and `% Hypervisor Run Time`; (4) inspect `Hyper-V Hypervisor Root Virtual Processor` and `Hyper-V Hypervisor Virtual Processor` counters to distinguish management/root and guest demand; (5) correlate `Processor\% Interrupt Time` and `% DPC Time`, VMQ/RSS, network/storage drivers, and device errors; (6) identify top VM workloads and guest application latency; (7) check firmware, power plan, clock/thermal throttling, effective processor count, and recent hardware/patch changes; (8) assess cluster headroom and migration safety; and (9) apply an approved workload, configuration, hardware, or placement change and verify sustained recovery plus service health.

Do not automatically migrate VMs, add/remove vCPUs, change processor compatibility/NUMA, change VMQ/RSS, switch power plan, update firmware/drivers, stop workloads, or drain/reboot a host from the alert. A saturated cluster may have no safe destination, and migration itself consumes resources. Changes require capacity model, workload ownership, redundancy/quorum, maintenance, rollback, and validation.

Review 7-, 30-, and 90-day recurrence and peak distribution for capacity planning. One sustained bucket supports incident triage; it does not alone justify hardware purchase or prove CPU caused a user symptom. Correlate demand growth, service SLOs, and cluster N+1 headroom.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot detector and counter failures

- **No Hyper-V object:** verify Hyper-V role/hypervisor launch, exact object availability through Performance Monitor/typeperf, Windows build, permissions, and reboot/change state.
- **Localized names or zero events:** verify `useEnglishOnly=1`, exact stanza, splunkd perfmon errors, source type, index route, and effective app precedence.
- **Values exceed 100:** reject from primary and compare raw counter, instance, formatting, field extraction, and aggregation. Do not clamp silently.
- **Only three samples:** source-health finding. Inspect forwarder/input cadence, host load, scheduler, queues, clocks, and indexing delay; do not infer below-threshold CPU.
- **Average high but minimum at or below 90:** expected no row. Use dashboards or a separately approved average/percentile capacity rule if business needs it.
- **One LP saturated while `_Total` is low:** expected exclusion. Add a per-LP imbalance rule with topology-aware persistence; do not alter `_Total` semantics.
- **Standard Processor differs:** expected on Hyper-V. Use the Hyper-V logical-processor counter for physical usage and root VP counters for management partition.
- **Alert clears while service remains slow:** CPU may have recovered or not be causal. Continue application, memory, storage, network, guest, and dependency diagnosis.
grandmaExplanation: We watch the Windows counter that shows how busy all physical processors on a Hyper-V host really are. If every collected reading stays above 90 percent for five minutes, we ask the host and service owners to investigate—but the alert does not decide which virtual machine or hardware setting caused it.
